overview: Theed is a planetary capital on Naboo, documented across Films · Clone Wars. Theed is Naboo's glittering capital of sandstone spires and plasma diplomacy, invaded by the Trade Federation and defended by Gungan alliance.
history:
Theed began as a planetary capital anchor on Naboo, positioned where water, ore, hyperspace lanes, or sacred geography forced travelers to stop. Theed grew where Naboo's resources—water, ore, kyber, or trade lanes—forced travelers to stop, creating a planetary capital that outlasted first founders. Early survey maps from the Old Republic era list Theed as a mandatory customs point for sector governors and Jedi exploration teams. Films, Clone Wars, Rebels, Mandalorian, Ahsoka, KOTOR, KOTOR II, TOR, and Sith Empire narratives all treat Theed as more than scenery—it is a decision point.

Ancient and pre-Republic layers beneath Theed include buried fortresses, Rakatan relics, and Sith ward-stones that still disrupt modern sensors. Pre-Republic and Sith-era layers beneath Theed include ward-stones, Rakatan markers, and Massassi masonry that modern engineers still discover during repaving. High Republic pathfinders logged Theed as a waypoint during the Great Hyperspace Rush, leaving beacon towers that later wars repurposed as artillery spotters. Local archives recovered from Naboo suggest Theed once governed trade policy for entire subsectors before centralization on Coruscant.

In the modern era, Theed expanded through prefab districts, orbital elevators, and refugee camps that fused multiple species into a single urban rhythm. Clone Wars, Imperial occupation, and New Republic rebuilding each added districts to Theed; Mandalorian and Ahsoka-era storylines treat it as a live operational hub. Mandalorian-era bounties and Ahsoka-era investigations repeatedly lead back to Theed because its ports lack the scrutiny of Core World bureaucracy. New Republic planners studied Theed as a template for rebuilding settlements after the Imperial collapse, citing both its failures and its innovations.

Theed has been invaded, liberated, blockaded, and rebuilt more times than most planetary capitals, making its streets a palimpsest of battle damage. Battle dossiers from KOTOR sieges, TOR planetary incursions, and Galactic Civil War raids mark Theed as strategically contested on Naboo. Clone Wars dossiers mark Theed as strategically vital; Imperial Era governors exploited that same geography to punish rebellious populations. KOTOR-era records and TOR-era campaign logs show earlier iterations of the same struggle—control of Theed meant control of Naboo.
significance:
The economy of Theed runs on layered industries: docking fees, black-market mediation, sacred tourism, factory output, or casino finance depending on the era. Theed's economy mixes legal trade with shadow finance—dock fees, kolto or tibanna exports, scavenging, or casino revenue depending on era and governor. Trade guilds from the Techno Union to the Mining Guild filed competing claims on Theed infrastructure during the late Republic. Post-war reconstruction funds often bypass Theed officially while flowing through its shadow banks—an open secret among Bothan analysts.

Cultural life in Theed mixes planetary tradition with imported habits from every species that ever missed a connection and stayed. Markets, cantinas, and temples in Theed blend Naboo native ritual with offworld imports, producing music and cuisine that signal rebel safe houses to trained eyes. Music, food, and festival calendars in Theed are used by rebels to signal safe houses and by Imperials to track dissident networks. Jedi historians note that some of the galaxy's quietest acts of mercy—evacuations, forged transit papers, hidden healers—were organized in Theed back alleys.

Theed influences galactic history disproportionately because leaders, smugglers, and prophets treat it as neutral ground until it suddenly is not. Treaties, betrayals, and superweapon strikes linked to Theed altered fleet movements across the Old Republic through Sequel Era conflicts. Scenes set in Theed across the saga often mark turning points: treaties signed, betrayals exposed, or the first shot of a regional war. Settlement planners across the Rim still cite Theed when arguing for open ports versus fortified capitals—a debate renewed after every occupation.
